This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the proposed model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the Time-Varying PAR with external covariates in real-world scenarios, we have developed multiple forecasting tools including model-based forecasting, forecasting of count-based outcomes, and forecasting of binary outcomes. Lastly, we have conducted a comprehensive simulation study to assess the statistical properties of the proposed method and an empirical application analyzing hospital injury data from the TraumMan study system.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the Quaker comet C/2013 A1 (Siding Spring) to enhance the precision of aerosol depth measurements to a precision of 0.01. This achievement allows for precise mapping of aerosols and dust devils on Mars, in addition to determining the optical depth of aerosols within a single report.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic forces and Brownian dynamics. A new study expands on previous work, carrying out a detailed investigation into the methods' performance when employed in Brownian dynamics simulations of biomolecules, with a spotlight on the impact of step size, the accuracy of configurational averaging, and the stability of equations. A novel numerical scheme, dubbed the composition avalanche integral method, was found to outperform existing techniques by significantly reducing errors resulting from small time step reservations in configurational averaging. This discovery led to the development of efficient Brownian dynamics simulations utilizing large time steps and significantly reducing the need for stochastic particle movement. As a result, substantial time savings can be achieved in simulations of biomolecules with minimal compromise in accuracy. A publicly available code was created to facilitate reproducibility.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties.

The paper reviews how non-standard, effective gauge sectors can generate novel phenomena by deviating from the conventional SM/2HDM approach. A bilepton model with a right-handed $W_R$ and $Z'$ vector boson is discussed, which interacts via a non-renormalizable, effective approach for processes beyond the tree-level. However, for purposes of theoretical construction, a UV-complete model with extra fermion fields is necessary. The review covers the production and decay mechanisms of bileptons, as well as recent research examining their potential signatures through radiative processes. The paper also examines the model's parameterization and the importance of higher-order calculations for matching bilepton decay widths. Additionally, the review delves into the implementation of the bilepton model within Monte Carlo event generators, which are a crucial step for simulating and analyzing its effects in laboratory experiments.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream. To accurately model the flame's behavior, the study accounts for heat release fluctuations that can lead to additional noise and instability in flames. The linear response of the flame can be visualized as the formation of quiet and noisy regions within the flame's structure, which then affects how the flame responds to vibration. To analyze these fluctuations, the study employs a linearized flame model that accounts for heat release, previously developed by de Ravendran, Sester, and Krebs, and incorporates it into an existing computational framework that simulates fluid dynamics and chemical reactions. The framework is then used to investigate the effects of methane concentration, fuel injection rates, and turbulence levels on the linear response of the flame to vibration. The results show that increasing the fuel injection rate or turbulence level can significantly enhance the flame's ability to detect vibrations, while increasing the methane concentration has a less pronounced effect. The study's findings also support the idea that wider fuel injection rates lead to more pronounced patterns of quiet and noisy regions within the flame's structure.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify the nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes (BH) within the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that an invisible population of BHs constitutes this population is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of DNA, polymers, and vortex fluids in planetary systems. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, the 4-move, the 5-move, the double-move, the hybrid-move, the sharp delta-move, the sharp gamma-move, the delta cross-move, the delta n-gon-move, the sharp n-gon-move, the gamma cross-move, the gamma n-gon-move, the 3-cross-move, the 3-gamma-move, the 3-delta-move, the 3-n-gon-move, the sharp 3-move, the delta 3-move, the gamma 3-move, the n-gon 3-move

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on situations where agents select between multiple tasks in an environment that is unknown. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there are only two options for each agent to consider over a wide-ranging quantity of linearly represented tasks. Furthermore, when there are multiple options available, a cooperative state can be defined as the most desirable through a linear programming optimization.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their large scale and massive MIMO characteristics, these systems can offer superior performance and coverage. With the significant gains in capacity and coverage, these systems present new opportunities for implementing wireless technology in various settings, including public hotspots and local networks. In densely populated areas with high user-densities, these systems can effectively reduce the number of necessary access points. As a result, less infrastructure is required to provide coverage in crowded environments. With fewer access points available to users, there is also a decrease in the amount of interference encountered.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that certain types of neural models actually inherit the knowledge of $N$-gram models and might reflect a reconstructed $N$-gram structure. We discovered that the computational cost of neural models is linked to how much they deviate from the $N$-gram model knowledge base and that this cost is directly reflected in language understanding tasks. Our research indicates that a simple $n$th-order bigram model provides a foundation for language understanding, outperforming higher-order models in many cases and sometimes even matching the performance of more complex neural models. Our results suggest that there's an optimal $n$-value for a given task, which can be determined based on the context size. We also found that pre-trained $n$th-order bigram models can enhance the performance of neural models on various tasks, which offers a straightforward way to improve models without additional training.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed in laboratory experiments and atmospheric data appear within two to five scale heights from the atmosphere's surface. In gas giant atmospheres, strong shear forces are present near the cloud layers, leading to the formation of multiple jet streams in both laboratory and atmospheric conditions. Thin film flows are observed in both laboratory and atmospheric conditions when there is a significant temperature difference between the equator and the poles. Thick film flows are more difficult to produce in laboratory experiments than in atmospheric conditions, as well as being more challenging to create near the surface of a planet.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations. Building upon this method, we've derived a closed set of hydrodynamic equations that are directly applicable to interacting Bose gases, bypassing the need for quantum field theory. This new approach offers a practical simulation tool for investigating a gas's quantum many-body effects in non-equilibrium situations, as demonstrated by applying it to a prototypical non-equilibrium model system consisting of interacting Bose gases and showing excellent agreement with existing benchmarks.

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures used in knowledge learning, exploring various knowledge-learning objectives and illustrating efficient implementations using lightweight student networks and soft/or pseudo-labels.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ variant equates to the centralizer $Z_{U(sl_2)}(\Delta)$ within the universal envelope $U(sl_2)$ encompassing the image of the diagonal embedding $\Delta$. As a result, generators and relations for the special Racah algebra are obtained. Additionally, a projection is defined that maps from the centralizer $Z_{U(gl_2)}(\Delta)$ to the special Racah algebra, thereby establishing a connection with the commutant of the diagonal embedding within the universal envelope $U(gl_2)$.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In an effort to fill this knowledge gap, our research focuses on analyzing the best actions to take in critical game moments by combining domain knowledge and artificial intelligence. We developed a deep learning-based framework that accurately predicts the most beneficial action for both attacking and defending teams across various situations on the soccer field. Through extensive testing on a large dataset of real soccer games, our network demonstrated a high level of accuracy in predicting actions that lead to goals, with an average precision of 25.6% and an average recall of 43.2% outperforming other machine learning algorithms. Notably, our findings reveal that passing the ball can yield significantly higher scores than shooting, with an average difference of 10.6% for the attacking team and 12.4% for the defending team. Our code is available on GitHub for public use.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is particularly relevant to scenarios where samples respond to various stimuli
and are often hard to reach locations. A simple yet effective method has been found
to guarantee precise measurement accuracy by calibrating the LDV system before
data collection commences. The document also includes two practical examples of
utilizing this setup within electromagnetic vibration measurement experiments and
molecular gas sensor experiments.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

To search for evidence of an unknown sector of particles that behaves similarly to the QCD axion, the Belle II experiment plans to analyze data resulting from the reaction $B^+ 	o K^+ E_i{}/$ through the process of particle decay, where an axion-like particle leaves the detector unobserved and an existing particle called an "echo axion" decays into a $KK\mu^+\mu^-$ final state. Based on five primary decay modes of the $B^+$ meson, an integrated luminosity of 50 fb$^{-1}$ is anticipated to yield approximately 10 events for a particle mass between 0.2 and 1 GeV that couples weakly to electroweak forces, assuming a particle charge of +1. For a charge of -1, the same luminosity is expected to yield around 3 events within the same particle mass range. To detect these events, Belle II plans to utilize a multivariate analysis tool called a "neural network" to differentiate between true events resulting from the described process and false positive outcomes caused by background radiation. To calculate the sensitivity of the Belle II experiment for detecting axion-like particles that behave similarly to the axion itself, physicists anticipate finding zero or one event resulting from the described process for an inferred particle density between 10$^{-2}$ and 10$^{-10}$ cm$^{-3}$ within the particle mass range of 0.2 to 1

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized embedding models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized embedding-based approaches, incorporating a broader
range of data sources and incorporating a category-specific lexical inventory
to improve results. Despite its enhanced performance, our findings reveal that
contextualized embedding models may misclassify words exhibiting little to no
semantic change, with approximately 7% of our corpus data matching this
characteristic. We argue that these inaccuracies stem from the models' tendency
to err when differentiating between semantically related words, given the
overlapping spectra of word meanings encoded within the contextualized
embeddings. We propose that this issue constitutes a significant challenge
preventing the accurate detection of diachronic semantic change using
contextualized embedding models, potentially leading to inaccurate results
as seen in our results.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting material and releasing enormous energy, permit the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra, as this research shows. By applying general relativity and incorporating multiple observational data sets, we can determine the parameters of two intermediate-mass black holes, with masses $20m_\sun < M_{\rm bh} < 50m_\sun$ and specific spins $>0.2$. This confirmation supports the spin-dependent growth of the spin-induced gap in the spectrum of AGNs, as predicted by theory, and also supports the spin-dependent growth of a milliradian-scale gravitational redshift in the spectrum of AGNs, as predicted by theory. Furthermore, we observe a positive correlation between the masses of black holes and the energies of jets in AGNs, which is consistent with previous findings, and also find that the most massive black hole identified in this study, with a mass of $40m_\sun$, exhibits the widest gravitational redshift feature detected thus far, with an angle of approximately $10^\circ$.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects.  We have developed multiple models that demonstrate varying levels of performance when using these conditional relationships and have conducted experiments showing that machine learning models can effectively learn new rules from text.  We have also created evaluation protocols to assess both the accuracy of models in mimicking established relationships and in generating novel ones.  Our findings reveal that despite the large size of the dataset, models do not suffer from overfitting when trained on all available information and that there is no significant performance disparity between models that have been trained on small subsets of the data and those that have been trained on the entire atlas.  Our results suggest that an infinite number of new rules can be accurately predicted from a single model without the need for additional training and that there is no significant difference in performance when generating narrow versus broad effects.  Our results also reveal that there is no substantial gap in performance when generating narrow versus broad effects.
