Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 56.3% respectively, without the use of prior views.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method was tested on pre-recorded datasets from various sources and showed significant improvements over existing approaches.  The findings suggest that by optimizing both the recording device and the analysis process, healthcare professionals can accurately diagnose heart conditions using cardiac auscultation sounds even in noisy environments.  The proposed framework provides a promising perspective for developing practical cardiac auscultation systems for clinical use.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation process to be heavily influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line formation model is independent of gas temperature, making it possible to determine gas masses using a CH2d model and an assumed temperature of 20K or by using CO lines if available.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges that highlights the critical role of context, drawing an analogy between model development and mathematical physics, versus physical chemistry, and commenting on the availability of model code on public repositories. Failing to account for stochastic effects in compartment-based models can be likened to omitting temperature in physical chemistry, as it may necessitate unrealistic assumptions similar to those concerning physical conditions. Failing to do so might also hinder the reproducibility of research, given the need for additional compartments to represent standard sources of randomness, such as demographic variability and sample sizes, when analyzing data empirically.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a significant decrease in their core rotation speeds due to conservation of angular momentum. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's core and its surrounding radiative zone exhibit distinctly different rotation periods, approximately 17.5 days for the core and 10.3 days for the outer zone. To explain this discrepancy, the star must have experienced internal mixing or an alternative angular momentum distribution, potentially induced by an unknown binary companion, g-mode oscillations, or an unresolved companion's tidal forces. To verify these hypotheses, future studies are recommended, focusing on g-mode oscillation patterns, the star's chemical composition, confirmation of the binary companion, and determining the star's actual angular momentum.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base called Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance to a conventional approach utilizing descriptive language when analyzing specific categories of knowledge. We also observe that pre-trained models with our method exhibit a significant reduction in training time compared to the conventional approach.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We present a comprehensive analysis demonstrating that all reconstruction challenges arise from solving a linear inverse problem for retrieving the Wigner function. By re-examining the mathematical foundations, we identify a straightforward, universally applicable method based on linear deconvolution for extracting the Wigner function from an optical tomogram. Utilizing this newly derived framework, we derive specific reconstruction formulas for different measurement schemes, including single-port and multi-port homodyne optical tomography. Our research provides a unified perspective on state reconstruction, offering a toolkit for implementing the linear inverse solution numerically. Our findings are further validated by applying the protocol to various examples, including coherent states, squeezed vacuum states, and a Mach-Zehnder interferometer based on a continuous-variable X-state.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our findings reveal that subsets defined by first-order logic are not recognisable by finite automata in base p/q systems, unless the denominator q=1. However, we do observe that subsets recognizable in base p/q systems match descriptions involving unbounded recursion in a function that is recognizable in base p/q systems.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems and their applicable domains, exploring various types of distance functions, including metric distances, semi-metric distances, and even certain types of distances in relational spaces. To better understand the connection between angle functions and Euclidean structure, researchers also delved into defining what it means for a space to be flat, in a manner analogous to the definition of convexity in geometry. Ultimately, this framework enables the application of convex geometry principles to spaces defined by angle functions, and allows for the solution to Menger's initially posed problems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation procedures for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements of 10 times in validation time and up to 10% in accuracy.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for creating and implementing such an integration plan, specifically for programs written in a recursive functional language that we have developed. This plan involves using geometric testing to guarantee safety testing, employ random testing to achieve coverage, implement a testing framework that leverages this structure, and apply formal verification techniques to verify the reliability of this framework. Our findings demonstrate that by employing our developed plan, we can create dependable software through a combination of mathematical proofs and actual testing.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that are prone to complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions within the self-sensing material.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations with minimal composite waste. 
The successful results indicate that the simple, cost-effective, self-sensing, and reusable technique comprising a physical model, EIT, and shape evolution optimization can be utilized to monitor damage growth and provide critical information for damage mitigation strategies in advanced composite materials.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating an additional iteration and derives directly through the Taylor series expansion of the inverse matrix. Theoretical analysis reveals that NN outperforms the Neumann Series and approaches the accuracy of Newton iteration, without requiring the inverse matrix of the input matrix. Furthermore, we derive a more efficient version called 'Nested Neumann with Kronecker Product' (NNKP) that offers improved convergence rates for large-scale matrices by incorporating a Kronecker product, along with an associated computational scheme. Theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical experiments conducted on various large-scale matrices generated from real-world applications, demonstrating the efficiency of the NNKP method in comparison to other fast approximate matrix inversion methods.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, contexts are assumed to be remotely located and only accessible via communication links. An approximately 5d contextual linear reward function can be estimated with a small error probability. This allows for near-optimal action choices with a context size of (2^d * log(d)) bits. This is significant as it indicates that only about 5d bits of context information are required on average. This is comparable to the information-theoretic limit of (2^d * log(d)) bits that can be obtained from samples of the reward function in an unconditional setting. This is a notable achievement as it marks the first time approximately 5d bits of context information can be learned with a small error probability in a decentralized contextual linear bandit problem. This is possible through the use of a linear feature representation of contexts and actions. This is in addition to the use of a linear reward function. This is in conjunction with an efficient learning algorithm that is based on the elimination of action options. This algorithm is capable of learning near-optimal actions with a small error probability in a decentralized contextual linear bandit problem. This is in a context where contexts are remotely

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 1 micrometer to 1 millimeter in particle size reduces the growth rate of VSI by three orders of magnitude. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement observed in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods to introduce hidden functionalities based on sensitive information such as user identity and location, thus bypassing current safety measures. What is even more concerning is the finding that these sophisticated backdoors can be created with only a small number of compromised training samples. In response, this paper proposes a new dynamic trigger idea called "Region-Based" and develops an efficient algorithm called "Differentiated Knowledge Embedding" to search for patterns within the activated region. Through comprehensive experiments, our method demonstrates significant improvement over existing research in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we conduct realistic scenario simulations to evaluate our model's ability to recognize patterns based on various input sources such as touch points and network addresses.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure that avoids this issue, and we also provide an alternative, simpler proof based on the concavity of variance for solutions in an infinite domain.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we provide an open-source implementation of the simulation-based validation process called "bfCheck." We conduct a series of scenarios to evaluate the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the impact of model complexity on the reliability of Bayes factors. Our findings suggest that Bayes factors can be unreliable in scenarios with low posterior odds and may not always reflect the true relative performance of models. We conclude that researchers should prioritize evaluating the reliability of Bayes factor estimates before making informed decisions about cognitive science theories. We also encourage the use

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, which can be found in the appendix. The results indicate that indicators closely correlate with discourse relations. The most frequently predicted indicators were then categorized and used to analyze the patterns associated with specific relations. Notably, indicators like "by contrast" and "however" are associated with contrastive relations, whereas "also" and "in addition" are linked to inclusive relations. The characterization provides a tool for evaluating the performance of research on predicting discourse indicators and classification tasks, which can be found in the appendix.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE system consisting of four LE sections with a 2-m focal length can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system can accurately determine the source direction with an accuracy of ~0.1 deg. The proposed MuLE optics system can be highly effective for use in future wide-field X-ray monitors on small satellites.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, significant improvements were not observed. To further this research, a series of dark matter simulation packages were generated with varying initial power spectra of density and velocity fluctuations. Results showed that when there are differences in the initial power spectra of velocity and density fluctuations, the inclusion of velocity information through a neural network can lead to more accurate halo mass predictions. Furthermore, when there are ratios of velocity to density fluctuations in the range of $0.5$ to $2$, the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology did not yield notable improvements. However, when the ratio of the power spectrum of velocity to density fluctuations is greater than or equal to $1$, the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology resulted in halo mass predictions through a neural network that were more accurate.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata to diagnose skin cancers. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, requiring an integration of image classification techniques and data preprocessing to handle unfamiliar lesions. To achieve this, an ensemble approach was employed combining CNN-based image classifiers, and a random forest to distinguish between known and unknown lesions. Furthermore, various data integration strategies were examined and applied to classify images based on their characteristics and metadata.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, and the Diagonal Lemma that follows from it. A concise, generalized proof of the first incompleteness theorem is provided, which serves as a foundation for subsequent discussions on the incompleteness of formal systems. A key contribution involves demonstrating that a formal system's incompleteness is not inherently linked to its consistency, as previously suggested by Godel. Instead, we establish an unconditional connection between incompleteness and the capability to encode arithmetic within the system. A historical analysis is also presented, focusing on the early 20th century developments in mathematics that led to the emergence of incompleteness theorems.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model that consists of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and the stability of the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability multipliers. An operator theoretical approach provides an efficient method to obtain the source estimate, which can then be used to construct a regularizer for the source term. An numerical example utilizing the finite element method in MATLAB confirms the stability result.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.
